findings.issue_text: Domain regex is not end-anchored, allowing subdomains such as user@trusted.com.attacker.net to bypass the whitelist
Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized, allowing case changes such as user@SPAM.COM to bypass a block for user@spam.com
Blocked-email match statistics are updated inside a failing User save transaction, so match_count and last_match_at updates are rolled back
match_count uses an unlocked read-modify-write sequence, causing concurrent matches to overwrite each other and lose increments

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: match_count uses an unlocked read-modify-write sequence, causing concurrent matches to overwrite each other and lose increments
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying issue: the race condition problem with updating match_count during concurrent operations. The golden comment frames it as 'side effects during a read operation' causing 'race conditions in concurrent environments', while the candidate specifically identifies the 'unlocked read-modify-write sequence' causing 'concurrent matches to overwrite each other'. Both are pointing to the same concurrency/race condition bug with the statistics update mechanism.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: Domain regex is not end-anchored, allowing subdomains such as user@trusted.com.attacker.net to bypass the whitelist
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same underlying issue: the domain regex pattern lacks proper anchoring/boundary checking. However, they describe the attack vector differently. The golden comment says an attacker can register 'evil.example.com' to bypass 'example.com' (subdomain of the whitelisted domain). The candidate says 'trusted.com.attacker.net' can bypass 'trusted.com' (whitelisted domain appears as subdomain of attacker's domain). These are actually opposite attack vectors - one exploits prefix matching, the other exploits suffix matching. The golden comment's concern is about suffix-only matching (domain appears at end), while the candidate describes a different vulnerability. The regex @(#{domains}) would match the domain anywhere after @, so both could be valid concerns, but they're describing different specific bypass scenarios.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: Blocked-email lookup is case-sensitive and unnormalized, allowing case changes such as user@SPAM.COM to bypass a block for user@spam.com
per_golden_matches.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same underlying problem as the golden comment: the case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block? allows users to bypass email blocks by using different letter casing. Both comments point out that variations like 'User@Example.com' or 'user@SPAM.COM' can bypass blocks set for 'user@example.com' or 'user@spam.com'. The core security vulnerability (case-sensitive comparison enabling bypass) is identical.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Blocked-email match statistics are updated inside a failing User save transaction, so match_count and last_match_at updates are rolled back

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real issue: BlockedEmail.should_block? in lib/validators/email_validator.rb updates match_count and last_match_at via record.save when validating an email. This validation runs during User model validation (validates :email, email: true). If the User save fails (which it will, since the email is blocked and an error is added), and if this happens within a transaction, the BlockedEmail statistics update would be rolled back. Looking at the code flow: EmailValidator.validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block? which does record.save to update statistics. This save happens during validation of the User model. If the overall User creation fails, any wrapping transaction would roll back these statistics. The spec tests BlockedEmail.should_block? in isolation, not within a User save context, so this issue wouldn't be caught.
